title: Voice, Body, Story
objective: Students will explore storytelling, voice, and embodied performance through the lens of the Harlem Renaissance oral tradition — the spoken word, the blues shout, the preacher’s cadence. They will develop and perform a short monologue, scene, or spoken word piece rooted in a Harlem Renaissance character or theme, and reflect on how performance creates empathy and historical understanding that written text alone cannot.
materials: Character cards — one per student or pair (on handouts)
Optional: audio of a Harlem Renaissance monologue or spoken word for model — recordings of Paul Robeson, Langston Hughes reading his own work, or a scene from a Zora Neale Hurston play
Open space for performance — desks cleared if possible; alternatively, students remain seated for in-class reading performances
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the exhibition:** Bring your class to experience the phonograph, the Great Migration Map, the Jazz Lab, and more. Ask your librarian to arrange a visit. **Option 2 — Virtual visit:**

steps.title: The body remembers
script: *“Before we talk about the Harlem Renaissance, I want you to do something. Stand up. Take up as much space as possible — arms wide, feet apart, chin up. Hold it for 10 seconds. Now make yourself as small as possible — shoulders in, head down. Hold it. Now stand normally and notice: which posture felt more like you? Which felt like a choice? The performers of the Harlem Renaissance made a choice to take up space — physically, artistically, politically. Today we’re going to explore what that means through performance.”*

steps.title: The oral tradition
script: The Harlem Renaissance had a rich oral performance tradition: **blues shouters** (Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey) who used the voice as an instrument of testimony; **preacher rhetoric** (Marcus Garvey, Adam Clayton Powell Sr.) using call-and-response with audiences; **spoken word and poetry readings** in Harlem salons and speakeasies; **theatrical performance** at venues like the Lafayette Theater.

steps.title: Step into a story
script: *“Zora Neale Hurston — folklorist, novelist, playwright — said the Black oral tradition was ‘the greatest cultural wealth of the American people.’ She spent years collecting the stories, the sermons, the songs. She believed that how a community tells its stories is as important as the stories themselves. Today you’re going to step into one of those stories.”*

steps.title: Choose a handout

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Receive a character card with background, situation, and sentence starters. Develop a 5–8 sentence first-person monologue. Practice with a partner, then share with the class (can be seated). Focus: speaking in first person and making one physical choice (gesture, posture).

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Choose a character from the provided list or create your own within the historical context. Write and perform a 60–90 second monologue. Must include one moment of silence (held pause) and one moment of vocal variety (volume, pace, or pitch change). Written reflection required.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Write and perform a 90–120 second monologue, scene for two voices, or spoken word piece. Must demonstrate: status awareness (how does your character hold power or lack of it?), subtext (what is the character not saying?), and one specific historical detail woven into the performance. Written dramaturgical note required.

steps.purpose: Write and perform a Harlem Renaissance voice at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.
